paras: The threatened lynching of Joe Battle took place in Edgecombe County, North Carolina, in November 1903, when officers heard that people meant to seize Battle, a Black man accused of assaulting a white woman near Rocky Mount, and lynch him. A deputy sheriff drove him to the Wake County jail in Raleigh on November 14 by a roundabout route, and he was held there until his return to Tarboro for trial in March 1904. North Carolina and Richmond papers followed the case through Battle's escape from the Raleigh jail, his recapture and his identification by the woman.

Battle was charged with assaulting Mrs. Bettie Long, a white woman of Edgecombe County, on about August 1, 1903; the Rocky Mount correspondent of the News & Observer described it as attempted rape. According to the News & Observer, a posse formed right after the alleged crime, but Battle got away to Virginia. On November 4, police in Manchester, Virginia, arrested him; the Times-Dispatch gave the charge as assault on 'a colored woman' and reported that Battle said he left Rocky Mount because people there 'looked like they were getting ready to do him some damage.' A telegram confirmed that he was the man wanted, and he was returned to Edgecombe on requisition papers.

Once Battle was back in the county, the News & Observer wrote, feeling 'again ran high', and officers heard 'intimations that an attempt would be made to get the negro and lynch him.' Deputy Sheriff B. R. Height took him out of Tarboro quietly and, understanding that sentinels had been posted along the way to head him off, drove more than 66 miles out of the direct road to Raleigh. The prisoner was put in the Wake County jail on the morning of November 14, to be held until the March term of the Edgecombe court. No report describes an actual gathering or an attempt on the jail or the road.

Early on January 5, 1904, Battle and eight other Black prisoners broke out of the Wake County jail; he and Len Spence were caught again early on January 7. On January 12 Mrs. Long came to Raleigh with her husband and Sheriff Bullock and identified him, saying, according to the Free Press, that he 'showed all signs of guilt.' The Times-Dispatch reported that he would stay in Raleigh because of the danger of lynching at Tarboro.

On March 4 the Edgecombe sheriff took Battle back to Tarboro to stand trial for his life before Judge Fred Moore, with 'considerable precaution' promised against interference. No report of the trial's outcome was found.

The coverage came entirely from white papers, led by the Raleigh News & Observer, whose headline 'Mob Wanted Rapist' treated the charge as settled and called Battle 'a bad looking negro'. It presented the lynching threat as a matter of high feeling and the deputy's detour as saving the man's life, without comment on the would-be lynchers; the Farmer and Mechanic reprinted the story two days later. State-news columns in the Monroe Journal and the Free Press repeated in a line that Battle was held in Raleigh because lynching was threatened.

The Richmond Times-Dispatch followed the case from the Manchester arrest to the March return, heading its last item 'The Danger of Lynching' and writing of preventing 'interference with the law taking its course.' The News & Observer's January jail-break story went further than its November report, stating that a mob 'was rapidly formed to lynch him' after the alleged crime and that 'again a mob formed' at Tarboro. No Black-press coverage of the case was found.

Battle's age was given as about 28 by the News & Observer in November, 22 in three January reports, and 15 in the Monroe Journal. The woman appears as Mrs. Bettie Long, Mrs. Paschal or Parschall Long, and, in one story, 'Mrs. Whitemore'; only the Manchester arrest item called her colored.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Joe Battle
bases: The episode is a threatened lynching: officers moved Battle, a Black prisoner accused of assaulting a white woman, out of Edgecombe County because they heard a mob meant to take and lynch him (A4, A7, A15).

No one was killed: Battle was taken to the Raleigh jail and later returned to Tarboro for trial (A4, A15); the would-be lynchers acted on an assault accusation, but their number is never given (A4, A8).

The News & Observer, the Monroe Journal and the Times-Dispatch each report, in separate items, that Battle was moved to Raleigh because a lynching was threatened (A4, A7, A13), though all trace back to officers' statements.

accounts.label: Deputy sheriff's account
accounts.gist: Deputy Height said feeling ran so high in Edgecombe that officers heard intimations of a lynching attempt, that he understood sentinels were posted to head him off, and that he drove 66 miles out of the direct road to save Battle's life.

accounts.label: Battle's statement at arrest
accounts.gist: Arrested in Manchester, Battle said he left Rocky Mount because the people there looked like they were getting ready to do him some damage.

accounts.label: Raleigh jail-break report
accounts.gist: The News & Observer wrote that a mob formed to lynch Battle right after the alleged crime, so he fled to Virginia, and that a mob formed again after he was returned to Tarboro.

framing.detail: The News & Observer headlined 'Mob Wanted Rapist', called the alleged offense a 'horrible crime' and Battle 'a bad looking negro', and presented the deputy's detour as saving the man's life, without comment on the mob.
The Times-Dispatch's Raleigh correspondent headed a March item 'The Danger of Lynching' and wrote of preventing 'interference with the law taking its course'.
Small North Carolina papers carried short state-news items repeating that Battle was held in Raleigh because lynching was threatened.

conflicts.note: The 15 in the Monroe Journal brief stands alone; 22 appears in three 1904 reports.
Long is consistent across five reports; 'Whitemore' appears only in the jail-break story.
Only the Manchester arrest item says the woman was colored; every North Carolina report, including the Edgecombe deputy's, says white.
The Rocky Mount correspondent wrote 'attempted rape'; later reports use rape or criminal assault.

versions.value: officers heard intimations of an attempt; sentinels understood to be posted

conflicts.note: The contemporary report rests on the deputy's hearsay; the jail-break story, written seven weeks later, states flatly that mobs formed.

record_check.dossier: Threat only is supported; no armed gathering is described beyond the deputy's understanding that 'sentinels' were posted, and the mob formations appear only in a later Raleigh story
